documents.publisher: AI Studio offline fixture, not a real publication
documents.text: Tardigrades are tiny animals, most less than a millimeter long, that live in moss, soil and water films. When their surroundings dry out, many species curl into a dormant state called a tun, and their metabolism drops to almost nothing. Given water again, a tun can revive and walk away, in some cases after years.

documents.title: Drying protection in tardigrades (offline fixture)
documents.publisher: AI Studio offline fixture, not a real publication
documents.text: Some tardigrade species make unusual proteins when they dry out. These proteins form a glass-like material that is thought to hold cell parts in place until water returns. How long a tun can survive is still debated, and record claims vary widely between studies.

segments.narration: Imagine your whole world drying up.
You are a tardigrade, a tiny animal less than a millimeter long, living in a film of water on moss.
As the water vanishes, you pull in your legs, curl into a dry little barrel called a tun, and your metabolism drops to almost nothing.
Inside your cells, special proteins might set into something like glass, holding everything in place.
Days pass. Then a raindrop lands. Given water again, a tun can revive and walk away, in some cases after years.
How long can a tun really wait? That question is still open. Follow IFNOVA for more strange science.
